newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany's builders on brink of pay strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany's builders on brink of pay strike.

text.p: Germany's troubled building sector moved a step closer to its first major strike since 1950 when the main wages commission of the IG Bau union on Monday urged union leaders to reject an arbitration-brokered pay deal.

"The union is prepared to resort to strikes to secure 100 percent sick-pay benefits for our members," IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt (IG Bau) head Klaus Wiesehuegel told a news conference after an intensive meeting at a Frankfurt hotel.
The decision will now pass to the union's board for a final decision on whether to reject or accept the deal. If the deal is not approved by May 21, IG Bau can lawfully call industrial action.
Wiesehugel said the union was prepared for further talks with employers. He also said that the union was prepared to compensate for the full payment of 100 percent of sick pay costs in wage talks.
"Our members are prepared to pay for their sick colleagues. It's a question of principles," said Wiesehugel.
The question of cutting sick pay to German workers has been at the centre of employer/union disputes in Germany in recent years.
Building sector employers said they were baffled by the decision to reject the pay deal. Strike action would be "catastrophic" for the construction sector, they said.
"Any subsequent strike would be a catastrophe for the recession-plagued construction industry," the ZDB and the BI, two employers' associations in the building sector, said.
Despite pleas from government officials not to strike, the commission had been expected to reject the deal, which was approved by a small majority in the arbitration committee.
The only winners if strike action were to be taken would be other European building groups with cheap labour who would take away badly-needed contracts from German firms, the employers' groups said.

Analysts believe any strike is likely to be limited since neither side can afford a prolonged dispute in a sector suffering from mass unemployment, with about 260,000 of its 1.3 million workers out of a job.
Officials from several regional units of IG Bau had signalled at the weekend that they were unhappy with the deal, which was reached last Thursday during a marathon negotiating session.
The controversial deal also recommended raising wages by 1.3 percent from last April 1 and reducing Christmas bonuses. German inflation stands at about 1.5 percent.
IG Bau had, among other demands, called for a wage increase of 2.9 percent and continued full pay during annual sick leave while employers sought to keep pay unchanged.
The employers' associations said that even in the event of being sick for six weeks, the employee would still have five weeks holiday left under the proposed changes.

Construction minister Klaus Toepfer warned on Friday that a strike would be "poison" for the troubled sector. He noted that new building orders in Germany had fallen by 8.7 percent in January and February.
Labour minister Norbert Bluem also warned of the potentially devastating consequences for the sector of a strike in view of the current weakness in the construction industry.
German employers meet at 0830GMT on Tuesday in Mainz to discuss the implications of the decision to reject the deal.
